title: Possession Has a Summer Release Date. That May Be the Remake’s Strangest Choice
dek: Parker Finn’s remake of Andrzej Żuławski’s Possession, starring Margaret Qualley and Callum Turner, is headed to theaters in summer 2027. A release slot built for scale will test whether the film’s ferocious intimacy can survive becoming an event.
content:
## A release date turns an experiment into a studio movie

Paramount has placed [Parker Finn](/people/parker-finn)’s new version of [*Possession*](/movies/possession-1981) in summer 2027, with reports specifying a June theatrical release. [Margaret Qualley](/people/margaret-qualley) and [Callum Turner](/people/callum-turner) lead the cast, while Madeline Brewer, Emory Cohen, Nicholas Alexander Chavez and Diego Calva have also been reported among the ensemble.

Until now, the project could be imagined primarily as a collision of sensibilities: the director of *Smile* taking on Andrzej Żuławski’s 1981 breakdown of a marriage, with two performers capable of making emotional instability feel physically dangerous. A summer date changes the frame. It tells exhibitors and audiences that Paramount sees more than an eccentric prestige remake. This is a movie expected to occupy meaningful theatrical space during the most competitive part of the calendar.

That confidence is understandable after Finn turned a disquieting grin into a durable horror brand. It is also the project’s central risk. The original *Possession* is memorable because it refuses the clean pleasures a broad release usually promises. It is domestic, political, grotesque and exhausting at once. Scaling that experience without domesticating it will be the remake’s real creative problem.

## The original resists a single genre label

Żuławski’s film begins with separation. Mark returns to West Berlin and finds that Anna wants to leave their marriage. From there, jealousy and surveillance open into bodily horror, doubles and an eruption in a subway passage that remains one of cinema’s most punishing performances. Describing the film as horror is accurate, but incomplete. It is also a divorce drama pushed beyond realism until private anguish contaminates every room and street.

Its divided Berlin setting is not decorative. Walls, checkpoints and empty spaces make intimacy feel subject to political pressure. The characters cannot separate cleanly because the whole environment is built around division. Remove that historical and geographic tension, and a remake needs another organizing pressure or risks retaining only the famous images.

This is why fidelity cannot mean duplication. Reproducing the apartment, the creature or the subway choreography would deliver recognition without necessity. Finn’s version has to discover what makes possession—of a partner, an identity, an explanation—feel urgent now. The original’s extremity came from the fact that its metaphors could not be neatly separated. A successful adaptation should create the same instability, not merely quote its symptoms.

## Margaret Qualley can make spectacle feel private

Qualley is a particularly suggestive choice because her performances can move between composure and rupture without making one look like the disguise for the other. That matters for a role inevitably shadowed by Isabelle Adjani’s work. The least interesting approach would be to treat the subway sequence as an acting challenge to be replicated and scored by intensity.

A remake earns distance by building a different body language from the beginning. Qualley’s precision could make smaller changes—the wrong pause, an over-controlled gesture, a sudden vacancy—carry the threat before the story becomes overtly impossible. Her task is not to compete with an iconic performance but to make comparison temporarily irrelevant.

Turner’s role is equally important. Mark can become a mere witness to Anna’s transformation if the film forgets that his need to understand and control her drives much of the violence. Turner has often played restraint as a form of pressure. If the remake preserves that mutual danger, the marriage can remain the engine rather than a runway leading to a creature reveal.

## Parker Finn knows how an image travels

The *Smile* films demonstrated Finn’s ability to build a campaign around an instantly legible visual idea. A smile works on a poster, in a trailer and in a public stunt before the audience knows the mythology behind it. *Possession* presents the opposite marketing problem. Its most recognizable moments are powerful because they are difficult to explain and dangerous to detach from the emotional descent surrounding them.

A summer campaign will be tempted to sell the remake through those images. The title itself invites a conventional supernatural promise, while the cast and budget can make the film look like an elevated horror event. Yet too much explanation would shrink the material. The original’s creature is not a puzzle answer that organizes everything preceding it; it makes the emotional reality even less stable.

Finn’s useful experience may therefore be structural rather than visual. He knows how to sustain dread across a studio horror narrative and how to make trauma more than backstory. The adaptation will reveal whether he can also leave contradictions unresolved—whether he can resist turning Żuławski’s fever into lore.

## Summer is a test, not a compromise

There is no rule that difficult cinema must open quietly in autumn. Horror audiences have repeatedly supported ambitious work in wide release, and a June date can give the film time to grow without being reduced immediately to awards positioning. Theatrical scale may even restore something essential: *Possession* is a confrontational communal experience, not a tasteful object meant only for private admiration.

But summer creates expectations about momentum, clarity and satisfaction. The remake will be measured against films designed to move efficiently through plot and against opening-weekend conversation that can flatten strangeness into approval or rejection. Paramount’s date says the studio believes the cast, filmmaker and title can withstand that pressure.

The most encouraging interpretation is not that *Possession* has been made safer. It is that the studio thinks its difficulty can be an attraction. That distinction will only become visible when trailers show what kind of film Finn has made.

## The date clarifies what remains unknown

The reported release window is concrete; most of the adaptation is not. Plot details, the new setting and the precise relationship to the 1981 screenplay have not been publicly established in the cited reports. It would be premature to assume that Qualley and Turner’s characters will reproduce every element of Anna and Mark, or that the film will preserve Cold War Berlin.

Those unknowns are more important than a familiar title. A remake of *Possession* should not reassure viewers that a cult object has been respectfully reconstructed. It should create the anxious sense that two people’s private disaster has escaped the terms available to describe it.

Summer 2027 is an audacious place to attempt that. The slot makes the film easier to see and harder to hide. If Finn and his cast preserve the original’s emotional danger while inventing a new reason for it, the release date will look less like a strange choice than a challenge issued to the mainstream audience.
